Daily Review Studio: Math

Daily Review Studio: MathStandards-aligned retrieval practice for Indiana classrooms

What are we practicing today?

Brief, standards-aligned retrieval practice for kindergarten through grade 5. Questions follow the Indiana Academic Standards and the question formats in Indiana's public item specifications.

Why brief daily review?
Retrieval practice strengthens memory. Recalling what was learned, rather than rereading it, improves long-term retention (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006), and the benefit holds in real classrooms across grades and subjects (Agarwal, Nunes, & Blunt, 2021). Practice testing and spaced practice are rated among the most effective learning techniques (Dunlosky et al., 2013).
Spaced, mixed review builds lasting skill. Returning to standards over time, and mixing problem types, helps students remember and choose the right strategy (Rohrer, Dedrick, & Stershic, 2015). Federal research guidance recommends spacing practice over time and using quizzing to support learning (Pashler et al., 2007).
Familiar formats let students show what they know. Practicing with the question formats described in Indiana's public item specifications keeps unfamiliar formats from getting in the way of showing understanding (AERA, APA, & NCME, 2014). Familiarizing students with item formats is a widely accepted practice (Mehrens & Kaminski, 1989).
It supports core instruction. Each page takes a few minutes and reviews standards students have already been taught. Every question is an original practice item; none are taken from state tests.
Sources
  • Agarwal, P. K., Nunes, L. D., & Blunt, J. R. (2021). Retrieval practice consistently benefits student learning: A systematic review of applied research in schools and classrooms. Educational Psychology Review, 33, 1409–1453.
  • American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education. (2014). Standards for educational and psychological testing. AERA.
  • Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58.
  • Mehrens, W. A., & Kaminski, J. (1989). Methods for improving standardized test scores: Fruitful, fruitless, or fraudulent? Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 8(1), 14–22.
  • Pashler, H., Bain, P. M., Bottge, B. A., Graesser, A., Koedinger, K., McDaniel, M., & Metcalfe, J. (2007). Organizing instruction and study to improve student learning (NCER 2007-2004). Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education.
  • Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255.
  • Rohrer, D., Dedrick, R. F., & Stershic, S. (2015). Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(3), 900–908.
